passage: Joseph carried folding chairs down to the courtyard of the Chennai housing society, where the meeting about the joint festival programme was about to begin. Reena, the treasurer, was counting steel plates. Two years ago Joseph had known only the lift button; last month, hearing the speakers crackle at the Pongal gathering, Joseph had offered to fix them. Tonight a resident asked, "Why must every festival be squeezed into one programme?" Joseph said, "Last year our Christmas star hung beside Mrs Iyer's kolam and nobody minded. I'd like to sing, and I'll bring the speakers." Reena wrote "sound: Joseph" on the sheet and looked up. "Come Saturday for the rangoli too." Joseph walked back up feeling that the whole building was, a little, home.

qa.q: What did Joseph offer to bring to the festival?
qa.a: Joseph offered to bring the speakers.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel about being part of the society now?
qa.a: Joseph feels included, walking back up with the sense that the whole building is a little bit home, after knowing only the lift button two years ago.

qa.q: How does Joseph show that belonging is built by showing up?
qa.a: By carrying chairs, fixing the speakers and offering time and skill for the shared festival.

qa.q: Why might the resident who asked about squeezing every festival into one programme have been unsure?
qa.a: The resident may have worried about crowding, and Joseph's example of the star beside Mrs Iyer's kolam shows differences sitting side by side.

grounding: The protagonist joins festivals and residents' meetings, contributes time and skills and respects differences, feeling at home through showing up.

passage: When I first moved into Shanti Nagar, Chandrika, I was a young woman of twenty-four and I didn't know a soul. I kept my door shut and ate dinner over the sink. Then the residents' association put up a notice for the Ganpati festival asking for someone to keep accounts. I could do sums, so I went. My hands were cold with nerves at that first meeting. Mr D'Souza from B-wing was treasurer; Farzana-bi from the corner house ran the food stall. For ten days I sat with the receipt book and learned everyone's name. Later that year, the same crowd helped put up the Christmas star on the gate, and at Eid Farzana-bi sent sheer khurma to every flat. Nobody made me believe what they believed. I just kept turning up. By the next year, Sudha-akka's ledger was the one they trusted.

qa.q: What task did the residents' association ask for help with during the Ganpati festival?
How did Sudha feel at the first meeting, and what showed it?
qa.a: Sudha felt nervous and shy, new to the colony; the cold hands at that first meeting show the nerves.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Sudha belong?
qa.a: Offering her skill with sums for the festival accounts and then turning up for each festival, whatever the faith.

qa.q: How might Farzana-bi have seen the new young accountant?
qa.a: Farzana-bi probably saw a quiet newcomer willing to help, and welcomed her by sharing food with every flat, including hers.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a young adult, she joined festivals and meetings, contributed her skills, and respected neighbours of other faiths until she belonged.

passage:
The Onam sadya at Lakeview Residency was set for noon, and at nine the rain began pouring through a tear in the courtyard tarpaulin. Nikita, who had joined the organising group only three months ago, stood in the downpour with Gargi, the society secretary, staring at eighty banana leaves getting soaked.
"The hall's booked by the Bohra families for a wedding lunch," Gargi said, rubbing her forehead.
Nikita thought of the rolls of clear sheet in her own storeroom from her set-design job. "Give me twenty minutes."
She came back with the sheets, a staple gun and two teenagers from D-wing. By eleven the courtyard was covered and dry. At the far end, she moved the sound speakers so the music wouldn't carry into the wedding lunch.
Eating rice off the leaf later, soaked to the knees, Nikita felt she was finally part of the place.

qa.q: What was the hall booked for?
qa.a: A wedding lunch by the Bohra families.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she ate the sadya at the end?
qa.a: She felt a warm sense of belonging and satisfaction, finally part of the place after helping save the event.

qa.q: What skills and choices helped Nikita contribute?
qa.a: She used the clear sheets from her set-design job to cover the courtyard, brought helpers, and moved the speakers so the music would not disturb the wedding lunch.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Nikita's help in the rain?
qa.a: Gargi was likely stressed and relieved, and may now see Nikita as someone the society can rely on.

grounding: The protagonist joins a housing society's festival, contributes her skills under pressure, and respects neighbours of another faith, building belonging by showing up.
